notes: Reasoning Ability topic package 2 for BATCH_008 (Month and Date-Based Puzzles, Puzzles (Other), Syllogism, Inequality): 50 original questions built by tools/packages/REAS_pkg2.py. Puzzles are brute-forced for a unique arrangement or recomputed with datetime; syllogisms checked over every Venn-region model; inequalities over every integer ordering (with a wider-range cross-check).

stimuli.title: Five colour words for comparisons
stimuli.content:
In the questions of this set, colour words are used between two letters with these meanings:
'A pink B' means 'A is greater than B'; 'A blue B' means 'A is smaller than B'; 'A red B' means 'A is either greater than or equal to B'; 'A grey B' means 'A is either smaller than or equal to B'; 'A green B' means 'A is equal to B'.
Assuming the statements to be true, find which of the conclusions I and II is/are definitely true.
stimuli.solution: Decode: pink means >, blue means <, red means ≥, grey means ≤ and green means =. Rewrite every statement with ordinary signs, join them into one chain and test each conclusion along it.

stimuli.title: Six exams on the weekdays of March 2027
stimuli.content:
Six exams — Chemistry, Hindi, Physics, Sanskrit, Statistics and Zoology — are held on six different dates in March 2027, one exam per date. No exam is held on a Saturday or a Sunday. 1 March 2027 is a Monday.

- The Statistics exam is on the first Wednesday of the month.
- The Physics exam is exactly 15 days after the Statistics exam.
- The Hindi exam is on the last Friday of the month.
- The Chemistry exam is on the same day of the week as the Physics exam, exactly one week earlier.
- The Zoology exam is on the first Monday after the Chemistry exam.
- The Sanskrit exam is on a date that is a multiple of 10, before the Hindi exam.
stimuli.solution:
Mondays of March 2027: 1, 8, 15, 22, 29, so Wednesdays are 3, 10, 17, 24, 31 and Fridays 5, 12, 19, 26. Statistics: first Wednesday, 3rd. Physics: 3 + 15 = 18th (Thursday). Hindi: last Friday, 26th. Chemistry: 18 − 7 = 11th (Thursday). Zoology: first Monday after the 11th, the 15th. Sanskrit: multiples of 10 are 10 (Wednesday), 20 (Saturday, no exams) and 30 (after Hindi), so the 10th.

Order: Statistics 3 (Wed), Sanskrit 10 (Wed), Chemistry 11 (Thu), Zoology 15 (Mon), Physics 18 (Thu), Hindi 26 (Fri).

stimuli.title: Seven book launches from April to October, in three genres
stimuli.content:
Seven authors Amit, Bhanu, Charu, Dhruva, Esha, Firdaus and Gunjan each launch one book in a different month from April to October of the same year. Each book belongs to one of three genres: Poetry, Fiction or Travel.

- No two books launched in consecutive months are of the same genre.
- Three of the books are Poetry, two are Fiction and two are Travel.
- Charu's book, a Poetry book, is launched in July.
- Esha's book is launched in the month immediately before Charu's, and it is not a Fiction book.
- Amit's book is launched in the first of the seven months and Gunjan's in the last, and neither of their books is Poetry.
- Firdaus's book is a Fiction book launched in a month that has 31 days.
- The two Fiction books are launched exactly four months apart.
- Bhanu's book is launched later than Dhruva's.
stimuli.solution:
Charu: July, Poetry. Esha: June; her book is not Fiction, and it cannot be Poetry next to Charu's Poetry July, so it is Travel. Amit: April, Gunjan: October, neither Poetry. Two more Poetry books are needed among May, August and September (April and October are not Poetry); August touches Charu's Poetry July, so May and September are Poetry. Firdaus (Fiction, 31-day month: May or August) therefore takes August, and Dhruva and Bhanu take May and September — Bhanu later, so Dhruva May, Bhanu September. The second Fiction book must be four months from August: April (Amit), since October is only two months away. Gunjan's book is then Travel.

Apr Amit (Fiction), May Dhruva (Poetry), Jun Esha (Travel), Jul Charu (Poetry), Aug Firdaus (Fiction), Sep Bhanu (Poetry), Oct Gunjan (Travel).

stimuli.title: Six bank branches and their opening years
stimuli.content:
A bank opened six branches — Alwar, Bidar, Churu, Dhule, Etah and Gonda — in six different years. The age of a branch in a year is the number of years completed since it opened (a branch opened in 2006 is 20 years old in 2026).

- In 2026, the Churu branch completes exactly 20 years.
- In 2026, the Alwar branch is exactly twice as old as the Churu branch.
- The Gonda branch opened seven years after the Churu branch.
- The Etah branch opened in a leap year, after the Churu branch but before the Gonda branch, and its age in 2026 is a multiple of 7.
- In 2026, the age of the Dhule branch equals the sum of the ages of the Gonda and Etah branches.
- The Bidar branch opened in the year in which the Alwar branch completed 10 years.
stimuli.solution:
Churu: 2026 − 20 = 2006. Alwar: 40 years old, 1986. Gonda: 2013. Etah: a leap year after 2006 and before 2013 is 2008 or 2012; ages 18 and 14, and only 14 is a multiple of 7: 2012. Dhule: 13 + 14 = 27 years, 1999. Bidar: Alwar completed 10 years in 1996.

Oldest to newest: Alwar 1986, Bidar 1996, Dhule 1999, Churu 2006, Etah 2012, Gonda 2013.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements:
All sardines are prawns.
Some lobsters are sardines.

Conclusions:
I. Some lobsters are prawns.
II. All prawns are sardines.

Take the statements as true. Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.explanation: The lobsters that are sardines are inside the prawns, so some lobsters are prawns (I). 'All sardines are prawns' cannot be reversed into 'All prawns are sardines' (II).
steps: Lobster ∩ sardine ≠ ∅ and sardines ⊂ prawns ⇒ some lobsters are prawns: I follows
All A are B does not give All B are A ⇒ II not certain
solution.why_others_wrong: Conclusion II is not forced by the statements (some valid diagram breaks it), so 'Both' and 'Only II' are wrong; I holds in every diagram, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements:
No fig is a peach.
All pears are peaches.

Conclusions:
I. Some figs are pears.
II. No pear is a fig.

Take the statements as true. Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.explanation: Every pear is a peach, and no peach is a fig, so no pear is a fig (II). That makes 'Some figs are pears' impossible (I).
steps: All pears are peaches + No peach is a fig ⇒ No pear is a fig (All + No = No)
II follows; I contradicts it
solution.why_others_wrong: Conclusion I is not forced by the statements (some valid diagram breaks it), so 'Both' and 'Only I' are wrong; II holds in every diagram, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements:

No turnip is a cabbage.

I. Some radishes are cabbages.
II. All cabbages are turnips.

Take the statements as true. Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.explanation: Some + No gives only 'Some radishes are not cabbages'. Whether any radish is a cabbage is open, so I is not certain. 'No turnip is a cabbage' makes 'All cabbages are turnips' impossible (II).
steps: Some radishes are turnips + No turnip is a cabbage ⇒ Some radishes are not cabbages (only this)
I: not certain
II: contradicts 'No turnip is a cabbage'
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion fails in at least one valid diagram, so 'Only I', 'Only II' and 'Both' are wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither conclusion I nor II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements:
All staplers are rulers.
Some rulers are markers.

Conclusions:
I. Some staplers are markers.
II. No stapler is a marker.

Take the statements as true. Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Either conclusion I or II follows

solution.explanation: The markers overlap the rulers, but not necessarily the part holding the staplers, so neither conclusion is certain. I and II are a complementary pair about staplers and markers: one of them must be true.
steps: All + Some ⇒ no definite stapler–marker link
'Some A are B' / 'No A is B' ⇒ complementary pair
Either I or II follows
solution.why_others_wrong: Neither conclusion is certain alone, so 'Only I' and 'Only II' are wrong; but in every diagram one of the two holds, so 'Neither' is wrong. ('Either' replaces 'Both' under the four-option rule.)
solution.final_answer: Option D: Either conclusion I or II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements:
Some temples are forts.
No fort is a palace.

Taking the statements to be true even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, which one of the following conclusions definitely follows?

solution.explanation: The temples that are forts can never be palaces, so some temples are not palaces (Some + No = Some not).
steps: Temple ∩ fort ≠ ∅
Forts are outside palaces ⇒ Some temples are not palaces
solution.why_others_wrong: 'No temple is a palace' and 'Some palaces are temples' are each possible but not certain (temples outside the forts are free); 'All forts are temples' is not given.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Some temples are not palaces.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Conclusions:
I. Some cables are not chargers.
II. All speakers being cables is a possibility.

Which one of the following sets of statements, taken to be true, makes both conclusions I and II definitely follow?

options.text: Some speakers are cables. All cables are chargers.
No speaker is a cable. Some cables are chargers.
All speakers are cables. No cable is a charger.
Only a few cables are speakers. All speakers are chargers.

solution.concept: Reverse syllogism: testing candidate statement sets
solution.explanation: With 'All speakers are cables. No cable is a charger.', no cable is a charger, so some cables are not chargers (I); and all speakers are cables, so II (a possibility) certainly holds.
steps: Test each set
Set 1: cables ∩ chargers = ∅ ⇒ I; speakers ⊂ cables ⇒ II
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Some speakers are cables. All cables are chargers.' makes I false; 'No speaker is a cable…' makes II impossible; 'Only a few cables are speakers. All speakers are chargers.' leaves the cables outside the speakers free to be chargers, so I is not certain.
solution.final_answer: Option C: All speakers are cables. No cable is a charger.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: Q > Z ≥ E = N ≥ U > H

Conclusions:
I. Q > N
II. E > H

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.explanation: All signs point the same way. Q > Z ≥ E = N gives Q > N (I), and E = N ≥ U > H gives E > H (II).
steps: I: Q > Z ≥ E = N ⇒ Q > N, true
II: E = N ≥ U > H ⇒ E > H, true
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion holds for every ordering that satisfies the statements, so picking one, or neither, is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both I and II are true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: T ≤ C < X > O = A ≥ Y

Conclusions:
I. T < A
II. Y < C

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.explanation: Both conclusions compare a term left of X with a term right of X, and the chain turns at X (C < X > O), so no relation is fixed.
steps: I: T ≤ C < X > O = A: turn at X ⇒ no relation
II: Y ≤ A = O < X > C: turn at X ⇒ no relation
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion fails for some ordering that satisfies the statements, so the other three are wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither I nor II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: M pink K, K red F, F green Z, Z grey S

Conclusions:
I. M pink Z
II. S pink K

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.concept: Decoding symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: M > K ≥ F = Z ≤ S. M > K ≥ F = Z gives M > Z (I). S and K are on opposite sides of the turn at Z, so S > K is not certain (II).
steps: Decode: M > K, K ≥ F, F = Z, Z ≤ S
Chain: M > K ≥ F = Z ≤ S
I: M > Z, true
II: K ≥ F = Z ≤ S: turn at Z ⇒ no relation
solution.why_others_wrong: II is not definitely true (a valid ordering breaks it), so 'Only II' and 'Both' are wrong; I always holds, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only I is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: E blue R, R grey N, N pink L, L green W

Conclusions:
I. E pink W
II. E blue N

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.concept: Decoding symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: E < R ≤ N > L = W. E and W are on opposite sides of the turn at N, so E > W is not certain (I). E < R ≤ N gives E < N (II).
steps: Decode: E < R, R ≤ N, N > L, L = W
Chain: E < R ≤ N > L = W
I: turn at N ⇒ no relation
II: E < R ≤ N ⇒ E < N, true
solution.why_others_wrong: I is not definitely true (a valid ordering breaks it), so 'Only I' and 'Both' are wrong; II always holds, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only II is true

Statements: G red B, B green V, V red Y, Y pink H

Conclusions:
I. G pink V
II. G green V

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Either I or II is true

solution.concept: Decoding symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: G ≥ B = V ≥ Y > H. Only G ≥ V is known; G > V and G = V are each uncertain, but one of them must hold.
steps: Decode: G ≥ B, B = V, V ≥ Y, Y > H
G ≥ B = V ⇒ G ≥ V
I (G > V) and II (G = V) split '≥' ⇒ either
solution.why_others_wrong: Neither conclusion is certain alone, but one of them must hold, so 'Neither' is wrong. ('Either' replaces 'Both' under the four-option rule.)
solution.final_answer: Option D: Either I or II is true

Chain: X ≤ T < D < J ≥ O
I and II cross the turn at J ⇒ no relation

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: F ≤ L; L < Y; Y = C; N ≥ C; W < F

Conclusions:
I. N > F
II. W < C

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.explanation: Combined: W < F ≤ L < Y = C ≤ N. All signs point one way, with a strict sign on each path, so N > F (I) and W < C (II).
steps: Chain: W < F ≤ L < Y = C ≤ N
I: N ≥ C = Y > L ≥ F ⇒ N > F, true
II: W < F ≤ L < Y = C ⇒ W < C, true
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion holds for every ordering that satisfies the statements, so picking one, or neither, is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both I and II are true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: R ≥ A; A = I; I > J; P ≤ J; P > V

Conclusions:
I. R > P
II. V ≥ J

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.explanation: Combined: R ≥ A = I > J ≥ P > V. R > P follows (I). J ≥ P > V gives J > V, so V ≥ J is false (II).
steps: Chain: R ≥ A = I > J ≥ P > V
I: R > P, true
II: J > V ⇒ V ≥ J false
solution.why_others_wrong: II is not definitely true (a valid ordering breaks it), so 'Only II' and 'Both' are wrong; I always holds, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only I is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: K < Z; Z ≥ O; O > H; H = B; E ≥ K

Conclusions:
I. E < Z
II. Z > B

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.explanation: Combined: E ≥ K < Z ≥ O > H = B. E and Z are on opposite sides of the turn at K, so E < Z is not certain (I). Z ≥ O > H = B gives Z > B (II).
steps: Chain: E ≥ K < Z ≥ O > H = B
I: turn at K ⇒ no relation
II: Z ≥ O > H = B ⇒ Z > B, true
solution.why_others_wrong: I is not definitely true (a valid ordering breaks it), so 'Only I' and 'Both' are wrong; II always holds, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: C > U; U ≤ M; M = Y; Y < Q; D ≤ C

Conclusions:
I. D > U
II. Q > C

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.explanation: Combined: D ≤ C > U ≤ M = Y < Q. D ≤ C > U turns at C, and Q > … ≥ U < C turns at U, so neither conclusion is fixed.
steps: Chain: D ≤ C > U ≤ M = Y < Q
I: D ≤ C > U: turn at C ⇒ no relation
II: C > U ≤ … < Q: turn at U ⇒ no relation
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion fails for some ordering that satisfies the statements, so the other three are wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither I nor II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: T ≥ K; K > W; W = E; S ≤ E; S > G; H ≤ T; H > B

Conclusions:
I. T > S
II. B < K

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.explanation: Combined: B < H ≤ T ≥ K > W = E ≥ S > G. T ≥ K > W = E ≥ S gives T > S (I). B < H ≤ T, then the chain turns at T (T ≥ K), so B and K are unrelated (II).
steps: Chain: B < H ≤ T ≥ K > W = E ≥ S > G
I: T > S, true
II: B < H ≤ T ≥ K: turn at T ⇒ no relation
solution.why_others_wrong: II is not definitely true (a valid ordering breaks it), so 'Only II' and 'Both' are wrong; I always holds, so 'Neither' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only I is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: N < Y; Y ≤ D; D = U; U < F; F ≤ X; R ≥ X

Conclusions:
I. R > Y
II. N < X

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.explanation: Combined: N < Y ≤ D = U < F ≤ X ≤ R. Every sign points one way and each path has a strict sign, so R > Y and N < X.
steps: Chain: N < Y ≤ D = U < F ≤ X ≤ R
I: R ≥ X ≥ F > U = D ≥ Y ⇒ R > Y, true
II: N < Y ≤ … ≤ X ⇒ N < X, true
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion holds for every ordering that satisfies the statements, so picking one, or neither, is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both I and II are true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: P > M; M ≥ J; J = A; A ≤ Q; Q < K; E ≥ P

Conclusions:
I. E > A
II. K > J
III. M ≥ Q

Which of the conclusions is/are definitely true?

options.text: All I, II and III are true
Only I and II are true

solution.concept: Three conclusions tested against one chain
solution.explanation: Combined: E ≥ P > M ≥ J = A ≤ Q < K. E > A (I) and K > Q ≥ A = J, so K > J (II). M and Q are on opposite sides of the turn at A, so M ≥ Q is not certain (III).
steps: Chain: E ≥ P > M ≥ J = A ≤ Q < K
I: E > A, true
II: K > Q ≥ A = J ⇒ K > J, true
III: turn at A ⇒ not certain
Only I and II
solution.why_others_wrong: 'All three' accepts III, which crosses a turn; 'Only I' and 'Only II' each miss a true conclusion.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only I and II are true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In which of the following expressions is 'G > T' definitely false?

solution.concept: 'Definitely false' means the opposite relation is forced
solution.explanation: In G ≤ L < R = T, G < T, so G > T can never hold. In each of the others G > T is possible for some values.
steps: 'Definitely false' ⇔ G ≤ T is forced
G ≤ L < R = T ⇒ G < T ⇒ G > T false
Others: the chain turns between G and T ⇒ G > T possible
solution.why_others_wrong: G ≥ L < R = T, T ≥ L = R ≤ G and G < L ≥ R > T all turn between G and T, so G > T may or may not hold — it is not definitely false.
solution.final_answer: Option A: G ≤ L < R = T

I. M > O

options.text: Neither I nor II is true
Both I and II are true

solution.explanation: Combined: M ≥ L ≥ Q < V = I ≥ R > O. M and O are separated by the turn at Q (Q < V); Q and R lie on either side of the turn at V = I. Neither conclusion is fixed.
steps: Chain: M ≥ L ≥ Q < V = I ≥ R > O
I: M … Q < V … O: turn at Q ⇒ no relation
II: Q < V = I ≥ R: turn at V ⇒ no relation
solution.why_others_wrong: Each conclusion fails for some ordering that satisfies the statements, so the other three are wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither I nor II is true

solution.concept: Use the month names and month lengths

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Hiral was born on the only date that occurs in leap years alone, so she celebrates on that date in 2028. Her brother Inder's birthday in 2028 is exactly 100 days after Hiral's birthday. 1 January 2028 is a Saturday.

On which date and day of the week is Inder's birthday in 2028?

solution.concept: Count days across months; use the leap day
solution.explanation: Hiral's birthday is 29 February. 1 January is a Saturday and 29 February is the 60th day of the year; 59 days later is 59 = 8 × 7 + 3 weekdays on: Saturday + 3 = Tuesday. Adding 100 days: March has 31 (to 31 March: 31 days), April 30 (61), May 31 (92), and 8 more days give 8 June. 100 = 14 × 7 + 2, so the weekday is Tuesday + 2 = Thursday.
steps: 29 Feb 2028: day 60; Saturday + 59 days ⇒ Tuesday
100 = 14 weeks + 2 days ⇒ Thursday
solution.why_others_wrong: 7 June miscounts the days by one; 8 June, Wednesday takes 100 days as 14 weeks + 1; 9 June, Friday starts counting from 1 March.
solution.final_answer: Option D: 8 June, Thursday

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Six volunteers Arnav, Bulbul, Chandan, Damini, Eklavya and Falguni each run a weekend camp in a different month from January to June 2026. 1 January 2026 is a Thursday, and 2026 is not a leap year.
- Bulbul's month has five Saturdays but only four Sundays.
- Damini's month has five Saturdays and five Sundays.
- Chandan's month has five Sundays.
- Falguni's month begins on the same day of the week as Chandan's month.
- Arnav's month comes after Eklavya's month.

Whose month begins on a Wednesday?

solution.concept: A month has five of a weekday only for the weekdays of its first (days − 28) days
solution.explanation: 1sts of 2026: Jan Thu, Feb Sun, Mar Sun, Apr Wed, May Fri, Jun Mon. A 31-day month has five each of its first three weekdays, a 30-day month of its first two, and February only four of each. January (Thu, Fri, Sat): five Saturdays, four Sundays — Bulbul. May (Fri, Sat, Sun): five Saturdays and Sundays — Damini. March (Sun, Mon, Tue): five Sundays — Chandan. Falguni's month begins on a Sunday like March: February. April and June remain, Eklavya earlier: Eklavya April, Arnav June. April begins on a Wednesday: Eklavya.
steps: 1sts: Jan Thu, Feb Sun, Mar Sun, Apr Wed, May Fri, Jun Mon
Five-of-a-kind days: Jan Thu–Sat, Mar Sun–Tue, Apr Wed–Thu, May Fri–Sun, Jun Mon–Tue
Bulbul Jan, Damini May, Chandan Mar, Falguni Feb
Eklavya Apr, Arnav Jun ⇒ Wednesday start: Eklavya
solution.why_others_wrong: Arnav's June begins on a Monday; Falguni's February and Chandan's March both begin on a Sunday.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Eklavya

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Six participants Nandini, Omesh, Pari, Qamar, Riya and Sahil took a quiz and got different scores (whole numbers).
- Exactly two participants scored more than Pari, who scored 47.
- Omesh scored 6 more than Riya and 4 less than Nandini.
- Qamar had the lowest score, 31, and the average of Qamar's and Riya's scores is 35.5.
- The highest score was 55, and Sahil scored more than Nandini.

Who has the fourth highest score?

solution.concept: Fix the values from the numeric clues, then rank
solution.explanation: Qamar 31 and Riya + Qamar = 71 give Riya 40, so Omesh 46 and Nandini 50. Sahil beats Nandini and the top score is 55, so Sahil 55 (no one else can reach 55). Pari 47 with exactly Sahil and Nandini above her. Order: Sahil 55, Nandini 50, Pari 47, Omesh 46, Riya 40, Qamar 31. Fourth: Omesh.
steps: Riya = 71 − 31 = 40; Omesh 46; Nandini 50
Sahil > Nandini and max 55 ⇒ Sahil 55
Order: Sahil, Nandini, Pari, Omesh, Riya, Qamar ⇒ fourth Omesh
solution.why_others_wrong: Pari is third, Riya fifth and Nandini second.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Omesh
